properties.title: Nuevo León y Coahuila (1856–1864)
properties.label: Nuevo León y Coahuila
properties.description: Santiago Vidaurri, the liberal strongman of Nuevo León, annexed Coahuila to his state in February 1856, and the 1857 Constitution recognised the union as the single state of Nuevo León y Coahuila. Vidaurri ran the northeast almost as an autonomous power, controlling the customs houses on the Rio Grande. When he refused to hand over their revenues in 1864, Juárez separated Coahuila again by a decree issued at Saltillo, and Vidaurri went over to the empire.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern states of Nuevo León and Coahuila. Their mutual boundary and the Coahuila–Chihuahua/Durango line have changed little, but the modern lines are only a stand-in.

sources.citation: Ronnie C. Tyler, Santiago Vidaurri and the Southern Confederacy (Texas State Historical Association, 1973).
H. Congreso del Estado de Nuevo León, Archivo, "Juárez se instala en Monterrey".
Constitución Política de la República Mexicana, sworn by the Constituent Congress on 5 February 1857 (arts. 13, 27 and 43).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Campeche becomes a state (1863)
properties.label: Campeche 1863
properties.description: A movement begun in the city of Campeche in August 1857 separated its district from Yucatán. The division of the peninsula was agreed in May 1858, and Campeche governed itself as a state from then on, but it was recognised by the federal government only in 1862 and became a state of the federation by a constitutional amendment of 29 April 1863. Much of the peninsula's east was still held by the rebel Maya of the Caste War.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern state of Campeche. Its eastern and southern limits in the 1860s ran through forest that neither state controlled; the modern lines with Quintana Roo (created 1902) and Guatemala (fixed 1882) are later.

sources.citation: Cristóbal Alfonso Sánchez Ulloa, "Celebraciones cívicas en la construcción de un estado: Campeche, 1857–1862", Secuencia no. 115 (Instituto Mora, 2023).
Richard N. Sinkin, The Mexican Reform, 1855–1876: A Study in Liberal Nation-Building (Institute of Latin American Studies, University of Texas at Austin, 1979).

properties.title: State of Hidalgo created (1869)
properties.label: Hidalgo 1869
properties.description: After the war Congress divided the huge State of México, which surrounded the capital. Its northern districts, around the silver town of Pachuca, which had been governed as a military district since 1862, became the state of Hidalgo in January 1869; the districts around Cuernavaca and Cuautla became Morelos three months later.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern state of Hidalgo, which descends directly from the districts separated in 1869. Dated to its promulgation by Juárez on 16 January 1869; accounts date the congressional decree to 15 January.

sources.citation: Richard N. Sinkin, The Mexican Reform, 1855–1876: A Study in Liberal Nation-Building (Institute of Latin American Studies, University of Texas at Austin, 1979).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).

properties.title: State of Morelos created (1869)
properties.label: Morelos 1869
properties.description: Congress erected the districts of Cuernavaca, Cuautla, Jonacatepec, Tetecala and Yautepec, the third military district of 1862, into the state of Morelos, named after the independence hero José María Morelos. It took in the sugar valleys whose haciendas would expand at the expense of village lands under the Porfiriato.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern state of Morelos, which descends directly from the districts separated in 1869. Congress passed the decree on 16 April 1869 and Juárez promulgated it on 17 April, the date shown.

sources.citation: Decreto de la erección del Estado de Morelos, Congreso de la Unión, 16 April 1869 (Consejería Jurídica del Poder Ejecutivo del Estado de Morelos).
Richard N. Sinkin, The Mexican Reform, 1855–1876: A Study in Liberal Nation-Building (Institute of Latin American Studies, University of Texas at Austin, 1979).

properties.title: Areas held by the republic, late 1865
properties.label: Republic, late 1865
properties.description: At the republic's low point in late 1865 the French and imperial armies held the cities, ports and main roads, and Maximilian's Black Decree assumed the war was over. Juárez's government survived at Paso del Norte on the US border, Juan Álvarez and his son Diego, the republic's governor of Guerrero, still held the Costa Chica, and Tabasco and Chiapas, under Gregorio Méndez, had kept their independence. Elsewhere the republic lived on as guerrilla bands in the Sierra de Puebla, Michoacán, the northeast and Sinaloa, which are not drawn as held territory.
properties.note: Hand-drawn and schematic: three areas that sources describe as in republican hands in October–December 1865, not a front line. Chihuahua City is left out (taken by the French on 15 August 1865, briefly republican again from 20 November to 9 December, and reoccupied on 11 December), and so is Acapulco (imperial from 11 September 1865). The Guerrero ring is anchored on La Providencia, Tierra Colorada, Ayutla, San Marcos, Ometepec and Cuajinicuilapa; northern Guerrero and the Costa Grande are not included for lack of a source. Tabasco–Chiapas follows the modern state outlines; imperial posts held out at Jonuta and at Carmen in Campeche. Contested guerrilla zones (Sierra Norte de Puebla, the Huasteca, the Tamaulipas–Nuevo León countryside, Michoacán's tierra caliente, Sinaloa) are not drawn. Clipped to modern Mexico.

sources.citation: Archivo del general Porfirio Díaz. Memorias y documentos, vol. II, ed. Alberto María Carreño (UNAM, Instituto de Historia / Elede, 1947), ch. LII, "Visita al general Álvarez en La Providencia".

Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, 1866, part III, doc. 41: Romero to Seward, 2 March 1866, enclosing letters of Gregorio Méndez from San Juan Bautista, 2 February 1866 (Office of the Historian, US Department of State).
Norma Zubirán Escoto, "Los ejércitos republicanos ante la Intervención Francesa", in La República errante (INEHRM, 2016), pp. 59–82.
Jorge Carrera Robles, "Benito Juárez en Paso del Norte", GacetINAH (Centro INAH Chihuahua, 2021).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Plan of Ayutla
properties.label: Plan of Ayutla
properties.description: Proclaimed at Ayutla by Colonel Florencio Villarreal with the backing of Juan Álvarez, the cacique of the Guerrero coast, and amended at Acapulco on 11 March by Ignacio Comonfort, the plan called for the removal of Santa Anna and a congress to write a new constitution. The revolt spread from the south across the country, and in August 1855 Santa Anna left the capital and went into exile for the last time.
properties.note: Marked at the town of Ayutla de los Libres. The amended plan was issued at Acapulco, about 85 km to the west.
properties.modern_place: Ayutla de los Libres, Guerrero, Mexico

sources.citation: Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Brian Hamnett, Juárez (Longman, 1994).
Richard N. Sinkin, The Mexican Reform, 1855–1876: A Study in Liberal Nation-Building (Institute of Latin American Studies, University of Texas at Austin, 1979).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Juan Álvarez chosen president at Cuernavaca
properties.label: Álvarez president
properties.description: A junta of representatives of the victorious revolution met at Cuernavaca and chose Álvarez as interim president. His cabinet brought the young liberals of the Reform into national office, among them Benito Juárez, Melchor Ocampo, Guillermo Prieto and Comonfort. Álvarez handed power to the more moderate Comonfort in December 1855.
properties.note: Marked at the centre of Cuernavaca.

sources.citation: Richard N. Sinkin, The Mexican Reform, 1855–1876: A Study in Liberal Nation-Building (Institute of Latin American Studies, University of Texas at Austin, 1979).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).

properties.title: Ley Juárez, Ley Lerdo and Ley Iglesias
properties.label: Reform laws 1855–57
properties.description: The Ley Juárez (November 1855) ended the special courts of the clergy and army in civil cases. The Ley Lerdo (June 1856) forced corporations to sell their real estate to tenants or at auction; it targeted the Church, but it also applied to the communal lands of Indian villages, which were broken up in many regions over the following decades. The Ley Iglesias (April 1857) limited parish fees.
properties.note: Issued by the government in Mexico City; marked at the Palacio Nacional.

sources.citation: Jan Bazant, Alienation of Church Wealth in Mexico: Social and Economic Aspects of the Liberal Revolution, 1856–1875 (Cambridge University Press, 1971).
Richard N. Sinkin, The Mexican Reform, 1855–1876: A Study in Liberal Nation-Building (Institute of Latin American Studies, University of Texas at Austin, 1979).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Zacapoaxtla revolt and the conservative risings at Puebla (1856)
properties.label: Puebla 1856
properties.description: A conservative rising under the banner of "religión y fueros" began at Zacapoaxtla in the Sierra Norte de Puebla in December 1855 and seized the city of Puebla in January 1856. Comonfort besieged and retook Puebla in March and then ordered the intervention of the diocese's property to pay for the campaign, a foretaste of the larger war to come. In October 1856 conservative officers under Joaquín Orihuela, among them Miguel Miramón, seized Puebla again and held it against a government siege until 3 December.
properties.note: Marked at the centre of Puebla. Zacapoaxtla, where the revolt began, lies about 110 km to the northeast.

sources.citation: Richard N. Sinkin, The Mexican Reform, 1855–1876: A Study in Liberal Nation-Building (Institute of Latin American Studies, University of Texas at Austin, 1979).
Walter V. Scholes, Mexican Politics during the Juárez Regime, 1855–1872 (University of Missouri Press, 1957).
Hemeroteca Nacional Digital de México (UNAM), description of the Boletín oficial (Puebla), no. 9, 10 November 1856.
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Constitution of 1857
properties.label: Constitution 1857
properties.description: The constituent congress called under the Plan of Ayutla produced a federal, liberal constitution with a single-chamber congress and a bill of rights. It wrote the principles of the Ley Juárez and Ley Lerdo into the constitution and did not name Catholicism as the state religion. Pius IX condemned the Reform legislation, and the bishops refused absolution to officials who swore the oath to the constitution unless they retracted. It also recognised Vidaurri's merged state of Nuevo León y Coahuila.
properties.note: The congress met in the chamber in the Palacio Nacional; the point marks the palace.

sources.citation: Constitución Política de la República Mexicana, sworn by the Constituent Congress on 5 February 1857 (arts. 13, 27 and 43).
Richard N. Sinkin, The Mexican Reform, 1855–1876: A Study in Liberal Nation-Building (Institute of Latin American Studies, University of Texas at Austin, 1979).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Plan of Tacubaya
properties.label: Plan of Tacubaya
properties.description: General Félix Zuloaga, in garrison at Tacubaya on the edge of the capital, proclaimed a plan annulling the new constitution. President Comonfort joined it, dissolved Congress and arrested Juárez, then president of the Supreme Court. When the conservatives disowned Comonfort in January 1858, he released Juárez and left the country; Juárez claimed the presidency as his constitutional successor and the conservatives named Zuloaga, beginning the Reform War.
properties.note: Marked at Tacubaya, then a separate town west of the city.

sources.citation: Will Fowler, The Grammar of Civil War: A Mexican Case Study, 1857–61 (University of Nebraska Press, 2022).
Brian Hamnett, Juárez (Longman, 1994).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Juárez sets up the constitutional government at Guanajuato
properties.label: Juárez at Guanajuato
properties.description: Escaping from Mexico City, Juárez established his government at Guanajuato under the protection of a coalition of liberal states of the Bajío and the west. With the conservatives in the capital, the war took on a clear geography: the conservatives held the centre and the army, while the liberals relied on state militias in the north, west and the Gulf coast.
properties.note: Marked at the centre of Guanajuato city.

sources.citation: Brian Hamnett, Juárez (Longman, 1994).
Will Fowler, The Grammar of Civil War: A Mexican Case Study, 1857–61 (University of Nebraska Press, 2022).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Battle of Salamanca
properties.label: Salamanca
properties.description: The conservative army under Luis Osollo and Miguel Miramón defeated the liberal coalition army of Anastasio Parrodi. The victory opened the Bajío and the west to the conservatives and forced Juárez to leave Guadalajara.
properties.note: Marked at the town of Salamanca; the fighting took place in the surrounding country.

sources.citation: Will Fowler, The Grammar of Civil War: A Mexican Case Study, 1857–61 (University of Nebraska Press, 2022).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).

properties.title: Mutiny at Guadalajara: "los valientes no asesinan"
properties.label: Guadalajara mutiny
properties.description: After news of Salamanca, part of the garrison of Guadalajara mutinied and held Juárez and his ministers prisoner in the government palace. When the soldiers raised their rifles, Guillermo Prieto stepped in front of Juárez and talked them down. The government left the city soon after and made for the Pacific coast.
properties.note: The Palacio de Gobierno of Jalisco, where the ministers were held. Some accounts date the scene to 14 March.

sources.citation: Brian Hamnett, Juárez (Longman, 1994).
Jasper Ridley, Maximilian and Juárez (Ticknor & Fields, 1992).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Juárez's government retreats to the Pacific (1858)
properties.label: Juárez to Manzanillo
properties.description: Juárez and his ministers moved from Guanajuato to Guadalajara in February 1858 and, after the defeat at Salamanca and the mutiny, south to Colima and the port of Manzanillo. With the conservatives holding the roads of the centre, the only way to reach the liberal stronghold of Veracruz was by sea.
properties.note: Straight lines between the documented stops (Guanajuato, Guadalajara, Colima, Manzanillo); the roads actually taken are not reconstructed, and the dates of the Colima and Manzanillo stops are given only to the month.

sources.citation: Brian Hamnett, Juárez (Longman, 1994).
Jasper Ridley, Maximilian and Juárez (Ticknor & Fields, 1992).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Juárez's voyage from Manzanillo to Veracruz (1858)
properties.label: Juárez's voyage
properties.description: From Manzanillo Juárez sailed to Panama, crossed the isthmus by the new Panama Railroad, and continued by way of Havana and New Orleans to Veracruz, where he arrived on 4 May 1858. The detour of several thousand kilometres through foreign ports shows how completely the conservatives controlled the interior.
properties.note: A schematic sea route through the documented ports (Manzanillo, Panama, Colón, Havana, New Orleans, Veracruz); the ships' actual tracks are not known here. The Panama–Colón leg was by rail. Gillingham (ch. 11) gives 5 May for the arrival at Veracruz.

sources.citation: Brian Hamnett, Juárez (Longman, 1994).
Jasper Ridley, Maximilian and Juárez (Ticknor & Fields, 1992).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Veracruz, liberal capital
properties.label: Liberal capital
properties.description: For almost three years Juárez governed from Veracruz. The port gave the liberals the customs revenues of the country's main harbour, a link to the outside world, and the protection of the coastal fevers, which repeatedly wore down conservative armies coming down from the highlands. The United States recognised the Juárez government in April 1859.

sources.citation: Brian Hamnett, Juárez (Longman, 1994).
Will Fowler, The Grammar of Civil War: A Mexican Case Study, 1857–61 (University of Nebraska Press, 2022).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Battle of Ahualulco
properties.label: Ahualulco
properties.description: Miramón defeated the army of the north under Santiago Vidaurri at Ahualulco, northwest of San Luis Potosí. It was the high point of conservative success in the field; the liberals lost battles but kept raising new armies from the states.
properties.note: Marked at the town of Ahualulco, San Luis Potosí; the battlefield lay nearby.

sources.citation: Will Fowler, The Grammar of Civil War: A Mexican Case Study, 1857–61 (University of Nebraska Press, 2022).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).

properties.title: First conservative siege of Veracruz
properties.label: Siege of Veracruz 1859
properties.description: Miramón, now conservative president, marched down from the capital to take Veracruz but had no means of blockading it from the sea. With yellow fever approaching and supplies short, he abandoned the siege by 29 March 1859.
properties.note: Marked just outside the walled city of Veracruz; the besiegers' lines are not drawn.

sources.citation: Will Fowler, The Grammar of Civil War: A Mexican Case Study, 1857–61 (University of Nebraska Press, 2022).
Brian Hamnett, Juárez (Longman, 1994).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Battle of Tacubaya
properties.label: Tacubaya 1859
properties.description: While Miramón was away at Veracruz, Santos Degollado's liberal army threatened Mexico City, but Leonardo Márquez defeated it at Tacubaya. Márquez then had prisoners shot, among them medical students who had been tending the wounded; the "martyrs of Tacubaya" earned him the name "Tiger of Tacubaya".
properties.note: Marked at Tacubaya; the fighting spread over the hills and haciendas of the western edge of the city.

sources.citation: Will Fowler, The Grammar of Civil War: A Mexican Case Study, 1857–61 (University of Nebraska Press, 2022).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Reform laws issued at Veracruz
properties.label: Reform laws 1859
properties.description: From Veracruz Juárez's government nationalised the property of the Church without compensation (12 July 1859), made marriage a civil contract, created a civil registry, secularised cemeteries and separated Church and state; freedom of worship followed in December 1860. The laws were meant both to destroy the conservatives' main financial backer and to raise money for the war.
properties.note: Issued by the government in Veracruz; marked in the city.

sources.citation: Jan Bazant, Alienation of Church Wealth in Mexico: Social and Economic Aspects of the Liberal Revolution, 1856–1875 (Cambridge University Press, 1971).
Brian Hamnett, Juárez (Longman, 1994).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Antón Lizardo and the second siege of Veracruz
properties.label: Antón Lizardo
properties.description: In 1860 Miramón tried again, this time with two armed steamers bought in Havana to blockade the port. Juárez declared them pirates, and on 6 March US Navy ships captured them at the anchorage of Antón Lizardo, south of Veracruz. Without control of the sea Miramón gave up the siege about 20–21 March.
properties.note: Marked at the village of Antón Lizardo; the ships were taken at the anchorage offshore on 6 March. Miramón's headquarters were inland at Medellín. Sources give 20 or 21 March for the end of the siege, so the feature is dated only to the month.

sources.citation: Will Fowler, The Grammar of Civil War: A Mexican Case Study, 1857–61 (University of Nebraska Press, 2022).
Brian Hamnett, Juárez (Longman, 1994).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: McLane–Ocampo Treaty: the Tehuantepec transit (1859)
properties.label: McLane–Ocampo transit
properties.description: Signed at Veracruz on 14 December 1859 by Juárez's minister Melchor Ocampo and the US envoy Robert McLane, the treaty granted the United States perpetual right of transit across the Isthmus of Tehuantepec and along two northern routes, from Camargo and Matamoros to Mazatlán and from Nogales to Guaymas, with the right to protect them with troops, in return for four million pesos. Gillingham argues that this near-protectorate secured US support at the decisive moment, when US warships seized Miramón's squadron off Antón Lizardo in March 1860. The US Senate rejected the treaty on 31 May 1860, so the transit was never used.
properties.note: Only the isthmus route is drawn, as a straight schematic line from Coatzacoalcos through Minatitlán and Tehuantepec to Salina Cruz; the treaty did not fix a line, and its two northern routes are not drawn.

sources.citation: Marcela Terrazas Basante, Los intereses norteamericanos en el noroeste de México. La gestión diplomática de Thomas Corwin, 1861-1864 (Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, 1990), ch. "Las presiones de McLane y su tratado".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Battle of Silao
properties.label: Silao
properties.description: Liberal armies under Jesús González Ortega and Ignacio Zaragoza routed Miramón at Silao in the Bajío. It was the turning point of the war: Guadalajara fell to the liberals that autumn, and the conservatives were driven back on the capital.
properties.note: Marked at the town of Silao; the battle was fought on the plain nearby.

sources.citation: Will Fowler, The Grammar of Civil War: A Mexican Case Study, 1857–61 (University of Nebraska Press, 2022).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).

properties.title: Battle of Calpulalpan
properties.label: Calpulalpan
properties.description: González Ortega's army defeated Miramón's last army in a two-hour fight on the hills of San Miguel Calpulalpan, northwest of the capital, taking its artillery, trains and thousands of prisoners. Miramón fled the country, and the liberal army entered Mexico City on 1 January 1861.
properties.note: Marked at San Miguel de la Victoria (formerly San Miguel Calpulalpan), Jilotepec, State of México. This is not the town of Calpulalpan in Tlaxcala, with which it is often confused. Gillingham (ch. 11) has González Ortega capturing Mexico City on Christmas Day 1860; the formal entry of the liberal army was on 1 January 1861.
properties.modern_place: San Miguel de la Victoria, Jilotepec, México, Mexico

sources.citation: Jesús González Ortega, parte de la batalla de Calpulalpan, Hacienda de San Francisco, 22 December 1860 (documento histórico, INEHRM).
Will Fowler, The Grammar of Civil War: A Mexican Case Study, 1857–61 (University of Nebraska Press, 2022).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Juárez returns to Mexico City
properties.label: Juárez returns 1861
properties.description: Juárez re-entered the capital ten days after his army. The liberals had won, but the country was bankrupt, conservative guerrillas still held the countryside, and in June 1861 they killed Melchor Ocampo, Santos Degollado and Leandro Valle near the capital.
properties.note: Marked at the Palacio Nacional.

sources.citation: Brian Hamnett, Juárez (Longman, 1994).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).

properties.title: Suspension of payments on the foreign debt
properties.label: Debt suspension
properties.description: With the treasury empty after the war, Congress suspended payments on the foreign debt for two years. Britain, France and Spain answered with the Convention of London (31 October 1861), agreeing to occupy Mexico's Gulf ports to force payment. Napoleon III had larger aims: a European-backed monarchy that would check the United States, then absorbed in its Civil War.
properties.note: Marked at the Palacio Nacional.

sources.citation: Michele Cunningham, Mexico and the Foreign Policy of Napoleon III (Palgrave, 2001).
Alfred Jackson Hanna and Kathryn Abbey Hanna, Napoleon III and Mexico: American Triumph over Monarchy (University of North Carolina Press, 1971).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Spanish, British and French forces land at Veracruz
properties.label: Allied landing
properties.description: A Spanish force under General Juan Prim occupied Veracruz and San Juan de Ulúa in December 1861 without resistance, and French and British contingents arrived on 7 January 1862. The coast in the fever season was deadly for European troops, which pushed the allies to seek a way up to the healthier highlands.
properties.note: Marked at the island fortress of San Juan de Ulúa in Veracruz harbour. Sources give different days in mid-December for the Spanish occupation, so it is shown only to the month.

sources.citation: Michele Cunningham, Mexico and the Foreign Policy of Napoleon III (Palgrave, 2001).
Alfred Jackson Hanna and Kathryn Abbey Hanna, Napoleon III and Mexico: American Triumph over Monarchy (University of North Carolina Press, 1971).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Preliminaries of La Soledad
properties.label: La Soledad
properties.description: Juárez's foreign minister Manuel Doblado and Prim agreed at La Soledad that the allies would recognise the government and negotiate, and in return could move their troops up to Córdoba, Orizaba and Tehuacán, out of the fever zone. If talks failed, they were to withdraw back to the coast before fighting.
properties.note: Marked at the town of Soledad de Doblado (then La Soledad), named after the agreement.

sources.citation: Michele Cunningham, Mexico and the Foreign Policy of Napoleon III (Palgrave, 2001).
Alfred Jackson Hanna and Kathryn Abbey Hanna, Napoleon III and Mexico: American Triumph over Monarchy (University of North Carolina Press, 1971).

properties.title: The allies split at Orizaba
properties.label: Orizaba 1862
properties.description: At a conference at Orizaba the allies broke apart: the French had brought conservative exiles, including Juan N. Almonte, under their protection and were clearly bent on overthrowing Juárez. Britain and Spain withdrew their forces, and the French stayed in the highlands they had reached under the terms of La Soledad.
properties.note: Marked at the centre of Orizaba.

sources.citation: Michele Cunningham, Mexico and the Foreign Policy of Napoleon III (Palgrave, 2001).
Alfred Jackson Hanna and Kathryn Abbey Hanna, Napoleon III and Mexico: American Triumph over Monarchy (University of North Carolina Press, 1971).
Jack Autrey Dabbs, The French Army in Mexico, 1861–1867: A Study in Military Government (Mouton, 1963).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Battle of the Cumbres de Acultzingo
properties.label: Acultzingo
properties.description: Advancing from Orizaba, General Lorencez's French army forced the steep pass of the Cumbres de Acultzingo against Zaragoza's rearguard and reached the central plateau. The way to Puebla, and beyond it Mexico City, was open.
properties.note: Marked at Acultzingo, at the foot of the climb; the fighting was on the pass above the town.

sources.citation: Jack Autrey Dabbs, The French Army in Mexico, 1861–1867: A Study in Military Government (Mouton, 1963).
Alfred Jackson Hanna and Kathryn Abbey Hanna, Napoleon III and Mexico: American Triumph over Monarchy (University of North Carolina Press, 1971).

properties.title: Battle of Puebla (Cinco de Mayo)
properties.label: Puebla, 5 May 1862
properties.description: Lorencez, expecting an easy victory, sent his columns up the Cerro de Guadalupe against the forts of Loreto and Guadalupe on the north side of Puebla. Zaragoza's army, with Porfirio Díaz's brigade on the flank, threw them back, and the French retreated to Orizaba to wait for reinforcements. The defeat cost Napoleon III a year and made the Cinco de Mayo a national symbol.
properties.note: Marked at the Fort of Loreto; the Fort of Guadalupe, the main target of the French assault, stands on the same ridge less than 1 km to the east.

sources.citation: Jack Autrey Dabbs, The French Army in Mexico, 1861–1867: A Study in Military Government (Mouton, 1963).
Alfred Jackson Hanna and Kathryn Abbey Hanna, Napoleon III and Mexico: American Triumph over Monarchy (University of North Carolina Press, 1971).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 12.

properties.title: French advance from Veracruz to Mexico City (1862–1863)
properties.label: French advance
properties.description: The French followed the old road from Veracruz through La Soledad, Córdoba and Orizaba, up the Cumbres de Acultzingo to the plateau and on to Puebla. Halted there in May 1862, they waited at Orizaba for a much larger army under General Forey, which took Puebla in May 1863 and then crossed the pass of Río Frío to Mexico City, occupied on 10 June.
properties.note: Drawn through documented places on the road (Soledad, Córdoba, Orizaba, Acultzingo, Palmar, Amozoc, Puebla, San Martín Texmelucan, Río Frío, Ayotla); straight lines between them. Individual columns and supply convoys also used other roads, which are not shown.

sources.citation: Jack Autrey Dabbs, The French Army in Mexico, 1861–1867: A Study in Military Government (Mouton, 1963).
Alfred Jackson Hanna and Kathryn Abbey Hanna, Napoleon III and Mexico: American Triumph over Monarchy (University of North Carolina Press, 1971).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Siege of Puebla
properties.label: Siege of Puebla 1863
properties.description: Forey's army surrounded Puebla, which Jesús González Ortega defended block by block for two months. With a relief army beaten and food exhausted, he surrendered on 17 May; the officers who refused to give parole were sent as prisoners to France, though some, Díaz among them, escaped on the way.
properties.note: Marked at the centre of the city; the fighting ran around its whole perimeter.

sources.citation: Jack Autrey Dabbs, The French Army in Mexico, 1861–1867: A Study in Military Government (Mouton, 1963).
Alfred Jackson Hanna and Kathryn Abbey Hanna, Napoleon III and Mexico: American Triumph over Monarchy (University of North Carolina Press, 1971).
Jasper Ridley, Maximilian and Juárez (Ticknor & Fields, 1992).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Battle of Camarón (Camerone)
properties.label: Camarón
properties.description: While escorting a convoy toward Puebla, a company of the French Foreign Legion under Captain Jean Danjou was surrounded by Mexican forces under Colonel Francisco de Paula Milán and fought from the buildings of a hacienda at Camarón until almost all were killed or captured. The fight shows how exposed the long French supply line through the coastal lowlands was; it became the founding legend of the Legion.
properties.note: Marked at the town of Camarón de Tejeda; the hacienda where the legionnaires fought stood at the town.

sources.citation: Douglas Porch, The French Foreign Legion: A Complete History of the Legendary Fighting Force (HarperCollins, 1991).
Jack Autrey Dabbs, The French Army in Mexico, 1861–1867: A Study in Military Government (Mouton, 1963).

properties.title: Battle of San Lorenzo
properties.label: San Lorenzo
properties.description: Ignacio Comonfort's army of new recruits, trying to break through to besieged Puebla with supplies, was surprised and routed by a French force under General Bazaine. With it went the last hope of relieving the city, which surrendered nine days later.
properties.note: Marked at San Lorenzo Almecatla (Cuautlancingo), northwest of Puebla; the exact battlefield is not located here.

sources.citation: Jack Autrey Dabbs, The French Army in Mexico, 1861–1867: A Study in Military Government (Mouton, 1963).
Alfred Jackson Hanna and Kathryn Abbey Hanna, Napoleon III and Mexico: American Triumph over Monarchy (University of North Carolina Press, 1971).

properties.title: French occupy Mexico City; Assembly of Notables
properties.label: French enter Mexico City
properties.description: Juárez left the capital on 31 May 1863 and the French entered it on 10 June. In July an Assembly of Notables chosen under French auspices declared Mexico a hereditary monarchy and offered the crown to Archduke Ferdinand Maximilian of Habsburg, who accepted it at Miramar in April 1864.
properties.note: Marked in the centre of Mexico City.

sources.citation: Alfred Jackson Hanna and Kathryn Abbey Hanna, Napoleon III and Mexico: American Triumph over Monarchy (University of North Carolina Press, 1971).
Jasper Ridley, Maximilian and Juárez (Ticknor & Fields, 1992).
Jack Autrey Dabbs, The French Army in Mexico, 1861–1867: A Study in Military Government (Mouton, 1963).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Juárez's itinerant government (1863–1865)
properties.label: Juárez's retreat north
properties.description: Juárez carried the republic north in a coach as the French advanced: to San Luis Potosí (June–December 1863), Saltillo (early 1864), Monterrey (April–August 1864, after a showdown with Vidaurri), then across the deserts to Chihuahua (October 1864) and finally to Paso del Norte on the US border (14 August 1865). By staying on Mexican soil he denied the empire the claim that the republic had ceased to exist.
properties.note: Straight lines between the seats of government. The leg from Saltillo to Chihuahua (August–October 1864, through the Laguna country) is schematic. Juárez returned briefly to Chihuahua in November–December 1865.

sources.citation: Jorge Carrera Robles, "Benito Juárez en Paso del Norte", GacetINAH (Centro INAH Chihuahua, 2021).
H. Congreso del Estado de Nuevo León, Archivo, "Juárez se instala en Monterrey".
Brian Hamnett, Juárez (Longman, 1994).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Maximilian and Carlota land at Veracruz
properties.label: Maximilian lands
properties.description: The new emperor and empress arrived on the Austrian frigate Novara to a cool reception in the liberal port and travelled up by Orizaba and Puebla to Mexico City, which they entered on 12 June 1864. Maximilian, a liberal himself, soon disappointed the conservatives by upholding the Reform's nationalisation of Church property.
properties.note: Marked at Veracruz.

sources.citation: Jasper Ridley, Maximilian and Juárez (Ticknor & Fields, 1992).
Alfred Jackson Hanna and Kathryn Abbey Hanna, Napoleon III and Mexico: American Triumph over Monarchy (University of North Carolina Press, 1971).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Siege and surrender of Oaxaca
properties.label: Oaxaca 1865
properties.description: Porfirio Díaz had made Oaxaca the main republican stronghold in the south. Bazaine brought a large army and siege artillery against it, and Díaz surrendered on 9 February 1865. He later escaped from prison in Puebla and returned to the field.
properties.note: Marked at the centre of Oaxaca. The French siege began in January; only the surrender date is shown.

sources.citation: Paul Garner, Porfirio Díaz (Longman, 2001).
Jack Autrey Dabbs, The French Army in Mexico, 1861–1867: A Study in Military Government (Mouton, 1963).

properties.title: The "Black Decree"
properties.label: Black Decree
properties.description: Believing that Juárez had left the country, Maximilian decreed that anyone captured with an armed band was to be tried by court-martial and shot within twenty-four hours. Republican generals José María Arteaga and Carlos Salazar were executed under it at Uruapan later that month, and the decree weighed against Maximilian at his own trial in 1867.
properties.note: Issued in Mexico City; marked in the centre. Some sources date the decree 2 October 1865.

sources.citation: Jasper Ridley, Maximilian and Juárez (Ticknor & Fields, 1992).
Alfred Jackson Hanna and Kathryn Abbey Hanna, Napoleon III and Mexico: American Triumph over Monarchy (University of North Carolina Press, 1971).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: The Matamoros cotton trade
properties.label: Matamoros trade
properties.description: During the US Civil War the Union blockaded the Confederacy's ports, but not the Mexican bank of the Rio Grande. Confederate cotton went overland across Texas to Matamoros and out through the beach anchorage of Bagdad at the river's mouth, and arms came back the same way. The trade made Matamoros briefly one of the busiest ports on the Gulf and made control of the northeastern border towns valuable to both empire and republic.
properties.note: Marked at Matamoros. Bagdad, at the mouth of the Rio Grande about 35 km to the east, has disappeared.

sources.citation: James W. Daddysman, The Matamoros Trade: Confederate Commerce, Diplomacy, and Intrigue (University of Delaware Press, 1984).
Ronnie C. Tyler, Santiago Vidaurri and the Southern Confederacy (Texas State Historical Association, 1973).

properties.title: Manuel Lozada and the autonomous canton of Tepic (c. 1857–1873)
properties.label: Lozada (Tepic)
properties.description: From the late 1850s the mestizo chief Manuel Lozada led the Cora, Huichol and mestizo villagers of the Sierra de Álica and the canton of Tepic (Gillingham uses the Cora and Huichol names, Náayari and Wixáritari) in defence of their lands and autonomy. He fought on the conservative side and then for Maximilian, who made him a general, and kept Tepic in practice independent of Jalisco; after 1867 Juárez tolerated it as a separate military district. In January 1873 his Plan Libertador sent his army against Guadalajara; beaten at La Mojonera, he was hunted down in the sierra and shot outside Tepic on 19 July 1873.
properties.note: Marked at San Luis (now San Luis de Lozada, Tepic), his headquarters. His following covered most of the canton of Tepic, roughly modern Nayarit, which became the Territory of Tepic in 1884; the start date is approximate (contemporaries in 1873 spoke of a movement more than fifteen years old).
properties.modern_place: San Luis de Lozada, Nayarit, Mexico

sources.citation: Regina Lira Larios, "Del Plan Libertador al fusilamiento de Manuel Lozada en 1873: el proceso de convergencia de una narrativa común sobre el lozadismo en la prensa de la Ciudad de México," Tzintzun. Revista de Estudios Históricos 70 (2019): 33–64.
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Battle of Santa Gertrudis
properties.label: Santa Gertrudis
properties.description: Republican forces under Mariano Escobedo destroyed a large imperial convoy and its escort travelling from Matamoros toward Monterrey. The defeat cost the empire its hold on the lower Rio Grande: Tomás Mejía's garrison surrendered Matamoros on 23 June, and the republic gained a border port open to supplies from the United States.
properties.note: Marked at the locality of Santa Gertrudis in the municipality of Camargo, Tamaulipas; the battlefield is not precisely located here.

sources.citation: Jasper Ridley, Maximilian and Juárez (Ticknor & Fields, 1992).
Alfred Jackson Hanna and Kathryn Abbey Hanna, Napoleon III and Mexico: American Triumph over Monarchy (University of North Carolina Press, 1971).

properties.title: Battle of Miahuatlán
properties.label: Miahuatlán
properties.description: Back in the field in Oaxaca, Porfirio Díaz defeated an imperial column at Miahuatlán in the southern sierra, then won again at La Carbonera later in October and retook Oaxaca City. The victories made him the dominant republican commander in the south and east.
properties.note: Marked at the town of Miahuatlán de Porfirio Díaz; the fighting was just outside it.
properties.modern_place: Miahuatlán de Porfirio Díaz, Oaxaca, Mexico

sources.citation: Paul Garner, Porfirio Díaz (Longman, 2001).
Laurens Ballard Perry, Juárez and Díaz: Machine Politics in Mexico (Northern Illinois University Press, 1978).

properties.title: The French army leaves Mexico
properties.label: French evacuation
properties.description: Under pressure from the United States after the end of its Civil War, and facing a rising Prussia in Europe, Napoleon III withdrew his army. Bazaine marched out of Mexico City on 5 February 1867 and the last French troops sailed from Veracruz on 12 March, leaving Maximilian to fight on with his Mexican army.
properties.note: Marked at Veracruz, where the army embarked.

sources.citation: Alfred Jackson Hanna and Kathryn Abbey Hanna, Napoleon III and Mexico: American Triumph over Monarchy (University of North Carolina Press, 1971).
Jack Autrey Dabbs, The French Army in Mexico, 1861–1867: A Study in Military Government (Mouton, 1963).
Jasper Ridley, Maximilian and Juárez (Ticknor & Fields, 1992).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Juárez returns south (1866–1867)
properties.label: Juárez returns
properties.description: As the French withdrew, Juárez left Paso del Norte for the last time in June 1866 and followed his advancing armies south: to Chihuahua, to Durango (26 December 1866), to Zacatecas, where a surprise raid by Miramón nearly captured him in late January 1867, and to San Luis Potosí, where he directed the last campaign. He re-entered Mexico City on 15 July 1867.
properties.note: Straight lines between the seats of government (Paso del Norte, Chihuahua, Durango, Zacatecas, San Luis Potosí, Mexico City).

sources.citation: Jorge Carrera Robles, "Benito Juárez en Paso del Norte", GacetINAH (Centro INAH Chihuahua, 2021).
Brian Hamnett, Juárez (Longman, 1994).
Jasper Ridley, Maximilian and Juárez (Ticknor & Fields, 1992).

properties.title: Battle of San Jacinto
properties.label: San Jacinto
properties.description: After his raid on Zacatecas, Miramón retreated south and was overtaken by Mariano Escobedo near the hacienda of San Jacinto, on the road between Zacatecas and Aguascalientes; his army broke within minutes of the republican charge. Many of the prisoners were shot, among them French soldiers who had stayed with the imperial army, and Miramón's brother Joaquín, captured wounded, was executed on 8 February. Miramón escaped to join Maximilian at Querétaro.
properties.note: Marked at San Jacinto, Rincón de Romos, Aguascalientes, the former hacienda of that name, near the Zacatecas state line; some sources place the battle in Zacatecas. Escobedo's report says he overtook Miramón at the hacienda of San Diego (Luis Moya, Zacatecas, about 14 km to the north) and pursued him toward San Francisco de los Adames, so the fighting spread across the modern state line.
properties.modern_place: San Jacinto, Rincón de Romos, Aguascalientes

sources.citation: Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, 1867, part II, doc. 377: Mariano Escobedo's report of the battle of San Jacinto (Office of the Historian, US Department of State).
Jasper Ridley, Maximilian and Juárez (Ticknor & Fields, 1992).
Miramón family papers, finding aid, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley (Online Archive of California).

properties.title: Díaz takes Puebla
properties.label: Puebla, 2 April 1867
properties.description: Porfirio Díaz's Army of the East stormed Puebla on 2 April 1867, and the forts on the Cerro de Guadalupe surrendered days later. Díaz then turned back Leonardo Márquez's relief force from Mexico City and laid siege to the capital, which surrendered to him on 21 June.
properties.note: Marked at the centre of Puebla.

sources.citation: Paul Garner, Porfirio Díaz (Longman, 2001).
Laurens Ballard Perry, Juárez and Díaz: Machine Politics in Mexico (Northern Illinois University Press, 1978).
Jasper Ridley, Maximilian and Juárez (Ticknor & Fields, 1992).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Siege of Querétaro
properties.label: Siege of Querétaro
properties.description: Maximilian went to Querétaro in February 1867 with the last imperial army and was besieged there by Escobedo's republican armies from early March. After failed attempts to break out, the city fell on 15 May, when Colonel Miguel López let republican troops into the Convent of La Cruz, the emperor's headquarters. Maximilian, Miramón and Tomás Mejía were captured.
properties.note: Marked at the Convent of La Cruz on the eastern edge of the old city. Sources date the start of the siege between 5 and 6 March.

sources.citation: Jasper Ridley, Maximilian and Juárez (Ticknor & Fields, 1992).
Alfred Jackson Hanna and Kathryn Abbey Hanna, Napoleon III and Mexico: American Triumph over Monarchy (University of North Carolina Press, 1971).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Execution of Maximilian at the Cerro de las Campanas
properties.label: Cerro de las Campanas
properties.description: Tried by court-martial under a republican law of January 1862 against crimes against the nation, Maximilian was shot on the Cerro de las Campanas with Miramón and Mejía, despite appeals for clemency from across Europe and the Americas. Juárez refused to intervene; the execution was a warning to any foreign power that might try to impose a ruler on Mexico.

sources.citation: Jasper Ridley, Maximilian and Juárez (Ticknor & Fields, 1992).
Brian Hamnett, Juárez (Longman, 1994).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: The Restored Republic
properties.label: Restored Republic
properties.description: Juárez returned to the capital in July 1867 ("among individuals as among nations, respect for the rights of others is peace") and was re-elected that year and in 1871. The Restored Republic cut the swollen army, completed the railway to Veracruz (1873) and restored constitutional government, but Juárez and Lerdo relied on managed elections and on loyal state governors.
properties.note: Marked at the Palacio Nacional.

sources.citation: Laurens Ballard Perry, Juárez and Díaz: Machine Politics in Mexico (Northern Illinois University Press, 1978).
Richard N. Sinkin, The Mexican Reform, 1855–1876: A Study in Liberal Nation-Building (Institute of Latin American Studies, University of Texas at Austin, 1979).
Brian Hamnett, Juárez (Longman, 1994).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Julio López's agrarian revolt at Chalco (1868)
properties.label: Chalco revolt
properties.description: Early in 1868 Julio López, a liberal colonel from the Chalco district at the southeastern edge of the Valley of Mexico, raised villagers against the haciendas that had taken their lands, water and woods, writing from the "headquarters of the defenders of the people". In March the district's villages petitioned Juárez to let him lay down his arms and to make the landowners show their titles, but government troops kept up the pursuit. He was eventually captured and shot, and the revolt became a founding episode for Mexican socialists; Gillingham describes its followers as calling themselves communists.
properties.note: Marked at Chalco, the head town of the district; the revolt moved through the villages of the Chalco and Texcoco area. Sources give 1868 or 1869 for López's execution, so the feature is dated only to the year; the revolt began in February 1868.
properties.modern_place: Chalco de Díaz Covarrubias, México, Mexico

sources.citation: Julio López, "Manifiesto," 23 February 1868, and "Carta al Presidente de la República de los habitantes de Chalco," 12 March 1868 (transcriptions, Historia Mexicana de los Planes e Insurrecciones, UNAM).
John M. Hart, Anarchism and the Mexican Working Class, 1860–1931 (University of Texas Press, 1978).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Plan de la Noria
properties.label: Plan de la Noria
properties.description: After losing the 1871 election to Juárez, Porfirio Díaz rebelled from his hacienda of La Noria in Oaxaca against indefinite re-election. The revolt was beaten, and Díaz's brother Félix was killed. It collapsed when Juárez died in the Palacio Nacional on 18 July 1872 and his successor Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada offered an amnesty.
properties.note: Marked at Oaxaca City; the hacienda of La Noria was on the outskirts of the city and is not located separately.

sources.citation: Laurens Ballard Perry, Juárez and Díaz: Machine Politics in Mexico (Northern Illinois University Press, 1978).
Paul Garner, Porfirio Díaz (Longman, 2001).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Battle of La Mojonera
properties.label: La Mojonera
properties.description: Lozada's army, advancing on Guadalajara under his Plan Libertador, was defeated by federal troops under General Ramón Corona at the Rancho de la Mojonera, on the outskirts of Zapopan. The rebels scattered into the sierra, and the defeat ended the autonomy of Tepic.
properties.note: Marked at the place called La Mojonera in modern Zapopan, northwest of Guadalajara; the battlefield is not precisely located here.

sources.citation: Thomas H. Nelson to Hamilton Fish, 15 February 1873, Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States, 1873, part I, vol. I, doc. 286.
Regina Lira Larios, "Del Plan Libertador al fusilamiento de Manuel Lozada en 1873," Tzintzun. Revista de Estudios Históricos 70 (2019): 33–64.
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.

properties.title: Plan of Tuxtepec
properties.label: Plan of Tuxtepec
properties.description: When Lerdo prepared to seek re-election, Díaz's supporters proclaimed the Plan of Tuxtepec at Ojitlán, in the Tuxtepec district of Oaxaca, under the slogan of no re-election; Díaz endorsed and amended it at Palo Blanco, Tamaulipas, in March. The revolt drew on regional chiefs and army officers across the country.
properties.note: Marked at San Lucas Ojitlán, where the plan was proclaimed; Tuxtepec, which gave it its name, is about 30 km to the east.

sources.citation: Laurens Ballard Perry, Juárez and Díaz: Machine Politics in Mexico (Northern Illinois University Press, 1978).
Paul Garner, Porfirio Díaz (Longman, 2001).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 11.
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 12.

properties.title: Battle of Icamole
properties.label: Icamole
properties.description: Díaz's own campaign in the northeast ended in defeat by government troops at Icamole, northwest of Monterrey. He slipped away to the United States and then by sea to Veracruz to rejoin the rebellion in the south, where his allies were winning.
properties.note: Marked at the village of Icamole (García, Nuevo León).

sources.citation: Laurens Ballard Perry, Juárez and Díaz: Machine Politics in Mexico (Northern Illinois University Press, 1978).
Paul Garner, Porfirio Díaz (Longman, 2001).

properties.title: Battle of Tecoac
properties.label: Tecoac
properties.description: Díaz, nearly beaten by the government army under Ignacio Alatorre, was saved by the arrival of Manuel González's division, and the Lerdist army broke. Lerdo fled the capital and Díaz entered Mexico City later in November, beginning the thirty-five years of rule known as the Porfiriato.
properties.note: Marked at Tecoac, near Huamantla, Tlaxcala; the battlefield extended across the surrounding plain.

sources.citation: Laurens Ballard Perry, Juárez and Díaz: Machine Politics in Mexico (Northern Illinois University Press, 1978).
Paul Garner, Porfirio Díaz (Longman, 2001).
